xref.title: Mayor Phil Givens Snubbed (1964)
xref.body: On September 6, 1964, Toronto mayor Phil Givens and his wife attempted to visit The Beatles at the King Edward Hotel at 1:30 pm but were turned away by a "blonde woman." She claimed two of the Beatles were sleeping and two were with relatives, an incident that led to the Daily Star publishing an article with the headline, "Beatles Blonde, Snob is Mayor." "The next day, the daily star released an article with the headline, Beatles Blonde, Snob is Mayor."

xref.title: Tax Exile in France (1971)
xref.body: In 1971, The Rolling Stones were forced to move to France as "tax exiles" because the British government was taxing 93% of their earnings, leaving them with only 7%. This event inspired the title of their album "Exile on Main Street." "In 1971, the Rolling Stones were required to pay 93% of all their earnings in taxes. They got to keep 7% of what they earned, 93%. And that's why they moved to France as tax exiles, which is why the next album was called exile on Main Street."

xref.body: Following the realization that their existing system was inadequate, The Grateful Dead's crew embarked on a year-long experimentation with PA gear, led by Owsley "Bear" Stanley. Their efforts culminated in the unveiling of the revolutionary "Wall of Sound" in 1973, a system designed to drastically improve live sound. "Over the next year, their crew experimented with PA gear, led by a former ballet dancer from Kentucky turned LSD drug dealer name Ausley Bear Stanley."

xref.title: Debut Performance at CBGB (August 14, 1974)
xref.body: On Wednesday, August 14, 1974, The Ramones played their first-ever show at the iconic New York club CBGB. The initial audience was sparse, consisting of fewer than a dozen people, including the club owner's dog. However, by the end of 1974, the band had performed at CBGB 74 times, with each gig progressively increasing their buzz. The club soon became packed with a diverse crowd, attracting Andy Warhol's circle, intellectuals, wealthy uptown youths seeking to "slum it," and music fans bored with existing sounds and looking for novelty. The Ramones' distinctive style — four "brothers" dressed in torn jeans and leather jackets, playing 1960s-style "bubble gum pop songs" at "a million miles an hour," without solos, stage interaction, or audience acknowledgment, pausing only when Johnny counted off the next song — marked the genesis of the New York punk rock revolution. "The Ramones played their first ever show at a New York club called CBGB."

xref.title: Bitter Split from Tony DeFries (April 1975)
xref.body: Following Bowie's decision to split from Tony DeFries, a 48-hour marathon negotiation took place in April 1975 to finalize his departure. The terms of the split were so harsh that it's said Bowie broke down and cried at the conference table, remaining in shock for a week. The agreement stipulated that Bowie could leave only if Main Man took half of his earnings from albums dating back to *Hunky Dory* in 1971 through an upcoming live album, and DeFries was guaranteed 16% of Bowie's gross earnings for the next seven years, through to 1982.

xref.title: Death by Heroin Overdose (February 2, 1979)
xref.body: Sid Vicious died at 21 years old from a heroin overdose. He was out on bail awaiting trial for the murder of his girlfriend Nancy Spungen. After 55 days in Riker's Island prison, a completely detoxed Sid was released on February 1, 1979, and celebrated his freedom with his mom Beverly, new girlfriend Michelle Robinson, and friends at Michelle's apartment at 63 Bank Street in New York. His mom called over English photographer and dealer Peter Codic to deliver heroin for him. Sid took a "taste" as a dessert, but due to his detoxed state, his body was super vulnerable to the 99% pure heroin, causing him to overdose. They revived him and put him to bed, which was a fatal move as he should have been kept awake until the drug left his system. The next morning, February 2, he was found stone-cold dead in bed next to Michelle. "Apparently the heroin he took the night before was 99% pure. And since he had detoxed, his body was super vulnerable."

xref.title: Fatal Overdose (1979)
xref.body: The night before his trial, on February 1, 1979, Sid attended a party in his honor at his new girlfriend Michelle Robinson's home, with his mother and friends present. His mother supplied him with heroin, and later he took more from her purse. He overdosed and was put to bed around 3 AM. No doctor was called to avoid violating his bail conditions. The next morning, he was found dead, naked, on top of the covers.

xref.title: Final Hours and Suicide (1980)
xref.body: On the evening of May 17th, Ian returned to his house at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, Manchester. His wife, Deborah, was working as a bartender at a wedding reception. They spoke, and Ian requested time alone, with Deborah agreeing not to return until after 10 AM the next morning, spending the night at her parents' house. After she left, Ian watched the 1977 film "Strozek," drank several cups of strong coffee and a shot of whiskey, and then wrote a long note to Deborah all night. As the sun rose on Sunday, May 18th, he put on Iggy Pop's "The Idiot," retrieved a rope from his garden's clothesline, and hanged himself. "Once she was gone, Ian sat down to watch his movie, which was a 1977 film entitled Strozek, which follows a musician and form a mental patient who travels to the US and is unable to decide between the two women in his life."

xref.title: Lineup Change and Stability (1986)
xref.body: In 1986, the same year Gord Downie graduated from Queens University, founding sax player Dave Manning left the band. He was replaced by Paul Langlois, who had first met Gord Downie in grade 11 and was the son of the school's gym teacher and football coach. With Langlois joining, the lineup of The Tragically Hip remained unchanged for the next 31 years. "The band was so crazy that the next day, 17,000 people turned up at an autograph session at a Los Angeles record store and a riot broke out."

xref.title: Murder in Seattle - July 7, 1993
xref.body: On July 7, 1993, Mia Zapata left the Comet Tavern in downtown Seattle around 1 AM, visited a friend, and then headed home with headphones on. Sometime within the next hour, she was beaten, raped, and murdered, found strangled with her hoodie cord at approximately 3:20 AM on the 100 block of 24th Avenue South. "On July 7th, 1993, Mia left a bar called the Comet Tavern in downtown Seattle. Sometime in the next 60 minutes she was beaten, raped and murdered. She had been strangled with a cord of her hoodie. A scream was heard at around 3 and then her body was found at about 320 on the 100 block of 24th Avenue South."

xref.title: "Mystery Days" Leading to Death (April 3-5, 1994)
xref.body: The three days between April 3 and April 5, 1994, leading up to Kurt Cobain's death, are largely considered a mystery, despite ongoing search efforts by a private detective and a missing person's report. During this time, Kurt was reportedly seen by various individuals around Seattle, including a taxi driver and friends, at a house he owned in Carnation, Washington, at a drug dealer's residence, and at several hotels. He also allegedly purchased a box of 20 gauge shotgun shells from a store called Seattle Guns. "The next couple of days, April 3, 4th, and 5th, 1994, are something of a mystery."

xref.title: Drug Overdoses and Jonathan Melvoin's Death (1996)
xref.body: Within six weeks of the Smashing Pumpkins' 1996 World Tour beginning, drummer Jimmy Chamberlain and touring keyboardist Jonathan Melvoin overdosed on heroin in Thailand in February, and again in Spain in May, narrowly escaping death. Jonathan Melvoin was subsequently fired but remained with the band until the tour concluded, while Jimmy was placed on "double secret probation." On July 11, 1996, just before two sold-out shows at Madison Square Garden in New York, Jimmy and Jonathan went to the East Village to purchase "red rum," a highly potent form of heroin. At 4 AM the next morning, Jonathan, who was ironically trained as an emergency medical technician, died from an overdose. Jimmy awoke from his stupor and called the police, leading to official statements being given within hours. "Jonathan Melvoin O.D. on heroin in Thailand."

xref.title: Dublin Concert Fatality (1996)
xref.body: During their World Tour for *Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness*, The Smashing Pumpkins played to about 7,000 people at the Point Theatre in Dublin, Ireland, on May 11, 1996. Seventeen-year-old Bernadette O'Brien rushed into the mosh pit and was crushed. Singer Billy Corgan stopped the show twice, first asking the crowd to cease crushing, then at 10:00 PM announcing the gig was over due to O'Brien being "nearly dying." O'Brien died the next day from massive internal injuries caused by the crushing weight. Her friend and two cousins were also injured but recovered. "I'm sorry, we can't play on, the gigs are over. There's a girl who's nearly dying. We, as human beings, cannot play up here while people are getting hurt down there."

xref.title: Magic Stick Assault (December 13, 2003) – Jack White Beat Von Bondies Singer Jason Stollsteimer
xref.body: On a Saturday night at the Magic Stick club in Detroit during the CD release party for a local band called Blanche, Jack White approached Von Bondies singer Jason Stollsteimer, spat in his face, and began punching him. When Stollsteimer fell to the floor, White continued hitting him until bystanders pulled him away. White filed a counter-complaint claiming self-defense. He initially pleaded not guilty, then changed his plea to guilty of misdemeanor assault and battery on March 9, 2004. Sentence: $500 fine, $200 court costs, one year of anger management. White maintained that Stollsteimer had grabbed him and pulled out his hair, and that his retaliation lasted less than 10 seconds. He also alleged that Stollsteimer refused to wash off the blood before posing for press photos sent to NME the next morning, and that the permanently damaged eye he claimed was a pre-existing injury from a contact lens incident as a teenager. White and Stollsteimer had not spoken for two years prior to the incident. "The entire event was completely exploited by him, his band and his managers and legal professionals."

xref.title: Death by Alcohol Toxicity (July 23, 2011)
xref.body: Amy Winehouse died tragically at age 27 on July 23, 2011, from alcohol toxicity, officially ruled a "death by misadventure." Her blood alcohol level was 0.416, more than five times the legal limit for driving, leading her to pass out, go into respiratory arrest, and fall into a coma. She was a deeply troubled woman, struggling with alcoholism, bulimia, and drug addiction. She had been diagnosed with emphysema in her mid-20s from crack cocaine use, leaving her lungs operating at only 70% capacity. She also had an irregular heartbeat, severe nicotine dependency, and recurring chest infections. In her final hours on July 22, 2011, she was in her Camden Square, London bedroom watching YouTube videos of herself and drinking heavily, after a two-week period of abstinence. Her live-in bodyguard, Andrew Morris, found her unresponsive the next afternoon. "Her blood alcohol level was 0.416. More than five times the legal limit for driving. Basically, she died of alcohol toxicity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Final Days and Alcohol Relapse (2011)
xref.body: Amy Winehouse was living at her home in Camden Square, London. On July 20th, 2011, her live-in bodyguard, Andrew Morris, joined her, tasked with keeping an eye on her. Over the next couple of days, Morris observed her drinking moderately, mostly vodka. By the evening of July 22nd, she had broken a period of abstinence and had been drinking "pretty hard" over the preceding two weeks, though Andrew Morris noted she seemed "fine" and her "usual bubbly self." "On July 20th, 2011, she was joined by her live in Bodyguard, guy with the name of Andrew Morris, who was supposed to keep an eye on her."

xref.title: Final Days and Discovery of Death (July 20-23, 2011)
xref.body: On July 20, 2011, her bodyguard found her appearing drunk, a relapse after a period of sobriety, and stayed with her. On the night of July 22, she was observed watching YouTube videos of her past gigs, laughing until 2 AM. The next morning, July 23, her bodyguard checked on her at 10 AM, finding her seemingly asleep. However, when he checked again at 3 PM, she was not breathing and had no pulse. Ambulances arrived at 3:54 PM, and she was declared dead shortly thereafter. "On the night of July 22, Amy stayed up late, watching YouTube videos of some of her past gigs. She seemed fine, laughing until about two in the morning."

xref.title: Secret Comeback (2011-2013)
xref.body: Bowie orchestrated his 2013 comeback album, *The Next Day*, in absolute secrecy. He worked with trusted producer Tony Visconti and a small coterie of musicians, all of whom signed non-disclosure agreements. His family and the skeleton staff at The Magic Shop studio (near his apartment) kept the secret. He had minimal staff, only his fiercely loyal personal assistant Coco Schwab and business person Bill Zysblat, with no pressure from his record label, Sony. His understanding of the internet meant he knew he could announce his return without a traditional marketing campaign, simply by dropping a hint online. "How did Bowie, one of the most famous musicians in the world that ever seen, manage that? He was working with Tony Visconti again. Tony can keep a secret."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Southwest Airlines Baggy Pants Incident (2011)
xref.body: On September 1, 2011, Billie Joe Armstrong of Green Day was removed from a Southwest Airlines flight from San Francisco to Burbank. A flight attendant chastised him about his baggy pants, and despite his protests, the attendant insisted he pull them up or be removed from the plane. xref.body: After facing disappointment with albums like "Tonight" (1984) and "Never Let Me Down" (1987), Bowie decided to "switch gears again" in 1988, recognizing that hard rock would move away from hair metal towards a more primal sound. xref.title: Lifelong Struggles with Mental Health, Drugs, and Alcohol
xref.body: Cornell grew up as a loner, one of six children raised by a single mother who was an alcoholic; his estranged father was also an alcoholic. He managed his mental health throughout Soundgarden's existence but after the band broke up in 1997 — coinciding with the failure of his first marriage — he went heavily into heroin and oxycodone. He entered rehab in 2002 and was entirely sober by 2005, except for prescription drugs. "No one really knows what one of the mill depression is. xref.title: Love Triangle and Intra-Band Feud
xref.body: In 1976, Joey Ramone met 16-year-old fan Linda Danielle from Queens at CBGB. They reconnected in Los Angeles a couple of years later and became a couple, with Linda joining The Ramones on tour. Johnny Ramone, who initially made Linda sit in the back of the van, eventually discovered common ground with her (neither drank or did drugs, she liked to cook, he liked home-cooked meals) and they became best friends. Joey and Linda became engaged, but after a dispute over a ring price, Johnny realized he was in love with Linda. Johnny intimidated Joey, who hated conflict, leading Linda to move towards Johnny over the next 18 months. They broke up, and Johnny and Linda became a couple in the early 1980s, marrying in 1984. "In 1976, just as the Ramones were starting to become known, Joey met a young 16-year-old fan named Linda Danielle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Meeting Max Kermann
xref.body: Nick Dica met Max Kermann on the second day of university, approaching him because Max was wearing a Sam Roberts Band T-shirt. After confirming his interest in music and ability to play bass, Nick was immediately invited to join the band. "And then the next day Nick introduced himself to me because I was wearing a Sam Roberts band T-shirt. And Nick said, I like Sam Roberts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mentorship by Brian Eno
xref.body: Brian Eno, impressed by a track Lanois produced for Time Twins, booked studio time with Lanois at Grand Avenue. Over several years, Lanois gained extensive knowledge about recording music while working on Eno's early ambient records. "Eno was so impressed that he booked time with Dan at Grand Avenue to work on some of his early ambient records and over the next couple of years Landwom learned a lot about recording music which he then applied to sessions with bands like Martha and the Muffins and the Parachute Club."

xref.title: Moroder's Influence
xref.body: Depeche Mode is one of the bands directly influenced by Giorgio Moroder's innovative use of synthesizers, particularly his work on Donna Summer's "I Feel Love." Moroder's robotic and futuristic sound laid a clear path for the emergence of technopop bands like Depeche Mode. "You can actually draw a straight line from that song through to Dopech mode and OMD and the human league and dozens and dozens of other technopop bands that would emerge in the next few years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Moroder's Influence
xref.body: The Human League is recognized as one of the technopop bands whose emergence was directly influenced by Giorgio Moroder's groundbreaking synthesizer experiments. His distinctive robotic and futuristic sound, exemplified by "I Feel Love," provided a clear inspirational blueprint for many groups in the electronic music scene. "You can actually draw a straight line from that song through to Dopech mode and OMD and the human league and dozens and dozens of other technopop bands that would emerge in the next few years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Musical Growth Over Time
xref.body: The band's sound evolved naturally from one record to the next, a direct result of their personal growth and changing musical influences, rather than a conscious effort for drastic change. Jared Followell, for example, grew from 15 years old on the first record to 21 on the fourth, naturally impacting their style. "It was just us growing musically. ...we've changed as people and musicians and our musical influences have changed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Nikolai Fraiture Backstage Incident
xref.body: During an early show where The Strokes opened for Girl Harbor at Don Hills, Nikolai Fraiture was caught having sex backstage in the basement and photographed. Girl Harbor then used this photo for a flyer for the next Strokes gig, with the caption, "this is what happened at our last show." "Nik was caught having sex backstage down on the basement and was photographed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Notable Contributors to Music
xref.body: Over the years, Jackalope's music featured contributions from a range of distinguished artists, including members of Sloan and Monster Magnet, Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails (who also co-produced), Alex Lifeson of Rush, and the three members named Don from Sons of Freedom. "Over the next few years, a number of really interesting artists contributed to Jackalope's music. The members of Sloan, the members of Monster Magnet, Trent Resner of Nine-H nails acted as a co-producer for a while. Alex Lifeson of Rush, and like I said, the three Don's from Sons of Freedom."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Bends Pressure and Hiatus
xref.body: After the success of "The Bends," Radiohead faced immense pressure to create an even better album, being compared to U2 and R.E.M. To cope, the band members scattered: Ed O'Brien went to India, Tom Yorke traveled solo in Europe, and others stayed home in England. They eventually regrouped in January 1996. "They were being called the next U2 and the next REM."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Crash Hiatus (10 Years)
xref.body: Following the devastating plane crash, Leonard Skinnerd remained absent from the music scene for ten years. Not all surviving members participated in the eventual reunion. "Leonard Skinnerd would remain absent from music for the next 10 years, and not everybody would be around for the reunion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producer Butch Vig Collaboration
xref.body: Following their signing with DGC, Nirvana spent nine months working on their new album, "Nevermind," with producer Butch Vig, a collaboration that proved instrumental in shaping their breakthrough sound. "The next nine months were spent working on a new album with producer Butch Vic."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pub Crawl Tradition
xref.body: The band has a tradition when they return home for Christmas after a tour, where they gather with friends at a pub, throw credit cards into a hat, and draw them to determine who pays the tab. The last two people drawn pay, and the process repeats at the next pub, excluding those who already paid, until everyone has contributed. "The song is based on how the band catches up with friends when they come home for Christmas after a long tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Quit Mod Robes, Sought Radio Job
xref.body: After watching the movie "Office Space," Ben abruptly quit his job at Mod Robes. He then contacted George Stroumboulopoulos, seeking advice on how to get a job in radio. "And I remember watching the movie Office Space and then the next day I went into mod robes and I quit. And I called George and I said, hey, I want to get a job at radio. How do I do it? How, where would I start?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Record Company Influence on Collaboration
xref.body: His record company, Virgin Records, prompted him to consider guest musicians for his next album because his deal was under review and a new record needed "some buzz." They specifically suggested he "call the Ashton boy[s]" (Ron and Scott) to work with him. "Iggy's deal with Virgin Records was under review. The next record had to generate some buzz or he would be dropped. And that's when it was quietly suggested that maybe Iggy round up some guest musicians for his next album."

xref.title: Recruitment by U2
xref.body: In 1984, U2 contacted Brian Eno to help them elevate their sound. When Eno agreed, he brought Daniel Lanois into the project, leading to "The Unforgettable Fire." "In 1984 Eno was contacted by U2 to help them take their sound to the next level and when Eno finally agreed to take the job he called up Dan and held it and the result was the unforgettable fire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Resonance of "Tragically Hip" Lyric
xref.body: During a Saturday Night Live performance of "Grace, Too," Gord Downie became overwhelmed by the line "I'm tragically hip," which resonated so deeply with him that his "inner elevator went from the penthouse to the basement," causing him to forget the subsequent lyrics. "He said I'm tragically hip and it was like, because I just resonated with him and my inner elevator went from the penthouse to the basement. I'd break next speed and I thought I don't even know the next line."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rivers Cuomo's Experimental Approach to Ratitude
xref.body: Rivers Cuomo embraced an experimental mindset for "Ratitude," telling the band, "this is just one more album out of many more that we're going to make." This indicated a willingness to take risks, suggesting that if an experiment didn't work out, they would simply try something different for the next album. "So in other words, if it works out great, if it doesn't, fine, we'll do something different for the next album."

xref.title: Secret Recording of "The Next Day"
xref.body: Bowie managed to record his album "The Next Day" in complete secrecy over two years in the internet age, a feat considered miraculous. This was achieved through the unwavering loyalty of his associates, who were sworn to secrecy, and by Bowie living a remarkably low-key life in New York City with Iman. He was often seen walking, grocery shopping, and attending social events, but people were accustomed to his flamboyant personas and simply didn't notice "David Jones." "How could one of the most famous musicians in the history of the universe manage to record an album in total secrecy in the age of the internet? It was a miracle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Shane MacGowan's Early Punk Anecdote
xref.body: Co-founder Shane MacGowan, a devoted hardcore punk fan, famously had part of his ear bitten off during a Clash show in 1976. A newspaper photo the following day captured Shane holding his ear in front of the stage with Joe Strummer towering above him, accompanied by the headline "Cannibalism at Clash Gig." "They were founded by Shane McGowan, a hard-drinking hardcore punk fan, who once had part of his ear bitten off during a clash show in 1976. The newspaper, the next day carried a photo of Shane holding his right ear in front of the stage with Joe Strummer towering above him, and the headline read Cannibalism at Clash Gig."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Speculated Divorce from Courtney Love
xref.body: It is speculated that Kurt and Courtney would have divorced at some point within five years if he had lived. "At some point over the next five years, he and Courtney would have been divorced."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Start with Hank Thompson
xref.body: On Halloween night in 1950, Ben Dorsi began a new job traveling with honky-tonk western performer Hank Thompson to help set up his gear. This role marked the start of his dedicated career as a roadie, a gig he would continue for the next six decades. "On Halloween night, 1950, he started a new job with Hank Thompson, a honky-tonk western performer, traveling with him to help him set up his gear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Studio Ownership and Academia
xref.body: Sylvia Massy owned her own studio for many years, which was a popular choice for bands like Sublime and Econoline Crush. Additionally, she has served as a visiting professor at Berklee College of Music and conducted workshops for the Abbey Road Institute, demonstrating her commitment to educating the next generation of audio professionals. "Sylvia owned her own studio for years, a place booked by Sublime, Econoline Crush and Dozens of Others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sudden Death Before Kubix Festival
xref.body: Paul Ryder died suddenly on July 15th at the age of 58. He had flown from Los Angeles to Manchester to play gigs with the band, complained of headaches upon arrival, went to bed, and was found by his mother the next morning, just hours before the band was scheduled to play the Kubix festival. "In July he flew in from his home in Los Angeles to play some gigs with the Mondays. When he arrived in Madchester he complained that he was having some headaches. He went to bed and never woke up. He was found by his mother on July 15th. Just hours before the band was supposed to play the Kubik's festival."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Surprise Album Releases
xref.body: Beyoncé became known for releasing albums without prior announcement in the 2010s, a strategy that David Bowie had pioneered with his 2013 album *The Next Day*. "I think Beyonce, who became known for doing this sort of thing. Did she do it before Bowie? Nope."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Target of "Screaming Mania"
xref.body: The Beatles became the subject of widespread "Beetlemania," with their female fans screaming intensely at their performances. This phenomenon followed earlier instances of screaming fans for Rudy Vallée and Frank Sinatra, marking a generational continuation of fervent fan devotion. "The next generation, the daughters of Valley fans, latched onto Frank Sinatra, and the grand daughters became screaming Beetlemaniacs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Target of Screaming Fans
xref.body: Frank Sinatra became a significant target of screaming female fans in the generation following Rudy Vallée. This "screaming mania" continued a pattern of intense fan devotion to popular male singers, preceding the phenomenon later seen with The Beatles. "The next generation, the daughters of Valley fans, latched onto Frank Sinatra, and the grand daughters became screaming Beetlemaniacs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The "Bohemian Rhapsody" Incident
xref.body: During their tour with Robert Plant, a fan dared The Trews on live radio to perform their old cover of Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" at a sold-out show in Rexall Place, Edmonton. The band delivered a "punky version" that garnered a standing ovation. This angered Robert Plant, who, having known Freddie Mercury, didn't want the past relived. He "accosted" their drummer, Sean, the next day in Calgary, but later issued a public apology by praising Canadian songwriters, including The Trews, at the Saddledome. "we got word that we really ticked Robert Plant off."

xref.title: The Thin White Duke Persona - Thomas Jerome Newton Influence
xref.body: This amoral, hollow, damaged, and emotionless character, with his signature white shirt and waistcoat, emerged from an autobiography Bowie began while filming "The Man Who Fell to Earth," in which he played the doomed space alien Thomas Jerome Newton. Bowie loved the character and asked to keep the costuming, directly influencing his look for the next couple of years. "This character came from a sort of autobiography Bowie had begun while filming the man who fell to Earth, the movie where he played a doomed space alien named Thomas Jerome Newton."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Theme Song for Degrassi: The Next Generation
xref.body: Jackalope composed and performed the theme song for the television series "Degrassi: The Next Generation" from season 4 onwards. "If you were a fan of Degrassi, the next generation, Jackalope did the theme song from season 4 onward."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ticketmaster Pricing Example
xref.body: The band is used as an example to illustrate the various fees that consumers encounter when purchasing concert tickets through Ticketmaster, including convenience charges, facility fees, order processing fees, and shipping charges. "Live Red Hot Chili Peppers. And the next time you want to go see them in concert and buy tickets to ticket master, you now know what kind of fees you're going to have to pay and where the money is actually going."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tour Routine
xref.body: John Wozniak described a typical tour bus schedule involving playing a gig, getting on the bus to sleep, waking up in the next town due to a driver, having a little free time for personal tasks or writing music, then sound check, dinner, interviews, and finally the next gig before repeating the cycle. The only saving grace mentioned were the minutes spent performing. "It's like you play a gig. You're done with the gig. You go to the van. You go wherever, hang out in the van. I mean, the bus. I'm sorry, I'm talking about a bus here. You jump on the bus, you sleep, and you wake up in the next town because there's a driver that drives you."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tour with Green Day (Later Career)
xref.body: Later in their career, after achieving sales of tens of millions of records, Blink-182 toured with Green Day, confirming Green Day's "elder statesman" role in the punk community. "And then the next time Green Day went on the road, it was with Blink 1 and 2, who were by this time selling tens of millions of records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tragic Miscarriage After "Gimme Shelter" Recording
xref.body: The day after her strenuous, late-night recording session for "Gimme Shelter," Mary Clayton suffered a miscarriage, losing her little girl. She believed the physical strain and late hour of the performance contributed to this tragic event, leading her to be unable to listen to the song for many years. "The next day, Mary miscarried. She and her husband lost a little girl, and Mary thinks it might have happened because of the lightness of the hour, and the strain she put on her body with that performance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transformation to "Godfather of Punk"
xref.body: Over 25 years after his initial struggles, Iggy Pop transformed from being "the most deranged man in rock" into one of the most respected figures, earning the title "Godfather of Punk" as his myth and legend grew. "Over the next 25 years, Iggy went from being the most deranged man in rock to one of the most respected. The Godfather of Punk and all that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transition to Horology
xref.body: After playing lead guitar for Anthrax for 15 years, Dan Spitz decided to dedicate his life to horology, the study, making, and repairing of timepieces. He earned a full scholarship to a Swiss watchmaking school, becoming certified as a mechanical complication specialist with degrees in micro-mechanical engineering, and later worked as an instructor for Chopard. "He was with the band for the next 15 years before he decided that he'd had enough and he was ready to dedicate his life to Horology."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unrealized Album Project
xref.body: David Botrell and Bob Lannwaw were slated to work on the next Psychedelic Furs record. However, the project did not proceed because the band had no songs written for rehearsal, and Lannwaw, having just spent a year and a half with an artist who wrote as they went, declined to continue. "Dan was slated to do the next psychedelic furs record and I went down with him to rehearse at John Giblin's rehearsal studio in Surrey"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Van Theft & Polish Mafia (Poland)
xref.body: While on tour in Poland one Christmas, NoMeansNo had their rented van stolen after a show in Warsaw, containing about $10,000 worth of merchandise. With local police being unhelpful and the Dutch rental company concerned about insurance coverage outside Holland, a fan connected them with the Polish Mafia. Band member Rob Wright met two heavily armed men in a church basement and negotiated the van's return for 2000 German marks. The next day, the van and all its contents were recovered from a barn outside Warsaw. However, the Warsaw police later demanded another 2000 German marks for operating outside legal channels. "The next day the van was given the name of a village about 100 kilometers outside of Warsaw and told to wait in the town square."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Wife and Lyric Inspiration
xref.body: Sarah Dylan, a model, married Bob Dylan in secret in November 1965. For the next dozen years, she served as the inspiration for the lyrics of many of Bob Dylan's songs. They divorced in 1977. "Sarah Dylan. They were married in secret in November 1965. And for the next dozen years, she inspired the lyrics for a number of Dylan songs. Then they divorced in 1977."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: World Tour with Inspiral Carpets
xref.body: For two years, Noel Gallagher toured the world with the Inspiral Carpets during what were described as some of the band's best years. In this role, he was responsible for looking after the guitars and gained invaluable experience in various aspects of life on the road, including customs, airports, hotels, crowd management, and the dynamics of a well-known band. "And for the next two years some of the best years of the Inspiral Carpets career. Noel toured the world with them looking after the guitars."
